claims.text: The bulk HfNbTaTiZr specimen contains 1 wt.% oxygen.
Oxygen atoms are randomly dispersed in the alloy and produce local lattice distortions.
Oxygen defects and their local strain fields may occur as clusters or as isolated scattering centers.
Defect-induced scattering dominates conductivity behavior from approximately 0 to 200 K.
Thermal activation and phonon scattering influence conductivity from approximately 300 to 1200 K.
Oxygen defects and their associated strain fields affect electron mobility.
A multiscale Monte Carlo simulation can generate statistically realistic oxygen-defect configurations and local strain fields.
Effective-medium theory can use the sampled configurations to estimate electron percolation and macroscopic electron transport.
Explicitly accounting for defect-laden microstructures overcomes limitations associated with analytical predictions for ideal crystals.
The proposed Monte Carlo and effective-medium approach will be significantly more accurate than conventional analytical models based on perfect crystals.
The predicted conductivity curve will exhibit a low-temperature plateau from approximately 0 to 200 K because of frozen defect-induced scattering.
The predicted conductivity curve will exhibit a thermally activated regime from approximately 300 to 1200 K in which phonon scattering is significant.
At approximately 350 K, the predicted conductivity will be within 20% of an experimental benchmark.
Traditional analytical conductivity predictions use perfect, defect-free crystalline models.
The proposed approach is restricted to bulk HfNbTaTiZr containing 1 wt.% oxygen and to the 0–200 K and 300–1200 K intervals.
Accuracy outside the stated oxygen concentration and temperature intervals is not assured.
The main uncertainties arise from parameterization of defect distributions and the fidelity of the effective-medium approximation.
A deviation greater than 20% between simulated and measured conductivity at approximately 350 K would falsify the hypothesis.
